You can already write software. You cannot read a note. That combination is more
common than the music-education world seems to think, and it's an unusually good
starting position, because most of what music theory describes is structure, and
you have spent years getting good at structure.

Sonic Pi normally gets introduced the other way round, as a way of teaching
programming through music. That works, but it moves slowly if you already know
what a loop is. Threads and arrays get the attention while harmony, melody and
rhythm wait offstage. Here, programming is the thing we already share. Arrays,
functions, state and concurrency are the tools, and music is the subject.

## What the book actually does

Each of the 58 lessons takes one musical idea, finds a representation for it,
and plays the result. Then you change one part and hold everything else still.
That small experiment is the whole method: a note moves, a cadence goes slack, a
rhythm shifts its weight, and now the explanation has something concrete to
account for.

The order follows what can be made concrete, not what is traditional. We start
with sound itself, then turn pitch and time into data. Acoustics explains why
certain relationships keep recurring. Rhythm, intervals, scales and harmony give
those relationships names. Notation shows up in Part 8, long after you can
already hear the things it notates, and transcription comes last of all. By the
capstones, that six-element array from Lesson 1 has grown into named voices
sharing a timeline. The representation grows because the music keeps asking more
of it.

Six decisions shape the course:

- **Sound first, name second.** You meet an interval, a cadence or a mode as
  something audible. The name shows up when it can help you recognise the thing
  again.
- **Music is data.** An event carries `:note`, `:start`, `:duration`, and
  sometimes `:amp`. Later fields describe articulation, spelling, or where the
  music came from.
- **Score and renderer stay apart.** The score says what happens. A playback
  function decides how it sounds. Changing instrument should never mean
  rewriting notes.
- **Examples end with music.** A test tone can isolate a fact. Only a phrase, a
  groove or a progression shows you what that fact does over time.
- **Notation arrives late.** The staff appears once pitch and duration are
  already familiar as numbers, so it can be treated as what it is: another
  coordinate system to decode.
- **Ear work runs alongside.** From Part 2 on, short drills ask you to recognise
  each new category without seeing its label, so the term has to answer to the
  sound.

Ruby idioms get a short explanation the first time they appear, and the whole
subset used here sits in [Ruby for
non-Rubyists](appendix/ruby-for-non-rubyists.qmd). Sonic Pi calls are in the
[cheat sheet](appendix/sonic-pi-cheatsheet.qmd). Every closing exercise has a
worked answer in the [solutions appendix](appendix/solutions.qmd), including
structural checks for the ones whose musical answer stays open.

This isn't a course in playing an instrument. It's an account of what musicians
organise and why, written in representations you can inspect, test, revise and
argue with. A program can't settle every musical question. It can make the
question precise enough to hear.

## Working rhythm

Four sessions a week gets you through the 58-lesson spine in about fifteen
weeks, with the capstones after that. The point of the schedule below is
spacing. New material needs to come round again before the next layer lands on
top of it.

| Session | Length | What |
|---|---|---|
| Two per week | 25 to 35 min | New lessons, in order. |
| One per week | 30 min | Consolidation. Rebuild a recent example from memory. |
| One per week | 30 min | Free play, using only ideas you've already met. |
| Most days | 10 min | Ear drills from your own `drills.rb`. |

Every fourth week, leave the new theory alone and rebuild a short phrase by ear
from material you already have. Once Parts 8 and 9 have given you notation,
source handling and a transcription workflow, that reconstruction can grow into
a properly sourced transcription. Something changes when a wrong value is what
stops a phrase from sounding like its source: the concept stops being a
definition to remember and becomes a diagnostic tool.

Run each example in a fresh buffer unless a comment says it continues from
above. Read the code once before you press Run, then listen without editing.
Make the variations one at a time. When pitch, timing and timbre all move
together, your ear has nothing clean to compare. And stop your live loops before
moving on, because they'll happily keep running while you switch buffers.

## About that "draft" label

Every lesson says `status: draft`. That means the concept, the exercise, the
explanation and a real Ruby example are all present, and the Ruby passes a
syntax check. It says nothing about what happens when you run the lesson in
Sonic Pi. Syntax checking confirms the shape of a program while missing an
invalid API call, a bad balance, or a description of the music that simply
isn't true.

A lesson reaches `tested` only when a person starts cold, works through it in
Sonic Pi, writes down where it breaks, and rewrites it from those notes.
Recordings come after that. Until then, timing, synth balance, API behaviour and
every claim about sound are waiting on a listener, and each lesson says so at
the top.

Keeping that visible is part of the method here. Code can parse perfectly while
the music it produces is wrong.
